answers.answer: In SCOPe 2.08 (latest periodic update 2.08-2026-08-16) the three structures do not give three different fold assignments. All of the syntaxin N-terminal-domain chains I checked are classified together, so the early fragments don't create a separate or misleading fold. Class a (all alpha), fold a.47 (STAT-like), superfamily a.47.2 (t-snare proteins), family a.47.2.1 (t-snare proteins), protein 'Syntaxin 1A N-terminal domain' (sunid 47663), species Rattus norvegicus. The members are d1br0a_ (1br0 chain A, NMR, sunid 17772); d1ez3a_, d1ez3b_ and d1ez3c_ (1ez3 chains A–C, sunids 17768–17770); and d1dn1b_ (1dn1 chain B, sunid 302344, the full domain in the Sec1/syntaxin complex). They are all a.47.2.1. 1dn1 chain A (d1dn1a_) is the Sec1/Munc18 partner, which is a different domain. It sits in e.25.1.1 under 'automated matches', a different class and fold, so the complex entry is split into domains with different classifications. A SCOPe domain is defined by the residue ranges of the actual chain or segment. In practice, an N-terminal-domain fragment that still carries the three-helix-bundle core, or a segment visible in a larger construct, is assigned to the same family as the complete domain when the shared structure supports it. This is a per-domain structural judgement, and the domain boundaries can differ between entries. Biological interpretation: (1) Fold, superfamily and family assignment from a fragment is acceptable only when the fragment keeps enough of the core to be unambiguous. Here that is the helical bundle, which is confirmed by the complete 1dn1 B domain at the same a.47.2.1 node. SCOPe's agreement of the fragments with the complete domain is what makes the fragment-based assignments trustworthy. It is not evidence that every fragment of every protein can be classified. (2) A shared family says the polypeptides are evolutionarily related and have the same N-terminal three-helix fold. It does not mean 1br0/1ez3 reproduce the full-length syntaxin conformation, the SNARE-motif/H3 region, or the closed Munc18-bound state seen in 1dn1. It also does not mean they share function, binding partners or regulation. NMR (1br0) versus crystal (1ez3, 1dn1) states, truncation, and oligomerisation or crystal packing can change helix packing and exposed surface, and so can change inferences about interfaces. (3) Fold-level (STAT-like a.47) membership is a structural grouping. It should not be used to infer homology to STAT, or SNARE function, outside the superfamily/family level. a.47.2 (t-snare) is the relevant evolutionary unit, and the fold is the broader structural grouping. (4) For template or representative selection, prefer the entry with the complete domain (1dn1 B) as the reference, and use the fragments only as supporting or alternative-conformation structures. Check PDB residue ranges, resolution, and any missing or truncated segments before using the fragments as templates. SCOPe is a classification, not an annotation of how complete or functionally relevant each structure is. Note that 1dn1 is flagged in the API as obsoleted by 3c98, so confirm the current PDB entry before relying on its coordinates. Limits: this answer rests on the 2.08 classification and live API records. I did not retrieve residue ranges or SCOPe comments for the individual domains, so I cannot say exactly which segments each fragment covers or whether SCOPe lists any explicit fragment note. I am describing the current assignments rather than stating the historical reclassification itself.
